title: Agents as first-class principals
summary: Register an agent, get its automatic keypairs, and exchange its API key for a short-lived JWT.

blocks.text: In 1Claw an agent is a real principal with its own identity, not a shared human login. An agent can authenticate three ways: an API key with the ocv_ prefix, mutual TLS, or OIDC federation. This lesson uses the API key path because it's the fastest to run end to end.

items: API key: ocv_ random value, argon2-hashed, shown once at creation
mTLS: client certificate identity for infrastructure agents
OIDC: federate an external identity provider into 1Claw

blocks.text: When you register an agent, 1Claw auto-generates an Ed25519 signing keypair and a P-256 ECDH keypair. Private keys live HSM-encrypted in the __agent-keys vault; only the public keys sit on the agent record.

steps.text: Use the same 1ck_ key from Foundations. Agent keys cannot create other agents.
Register an agent. The plaintext ocv_ key is returned once in this response and never again. Use the vault UUID from Foundations (`1claw vault list`) and export it: `export VAULT_ID=...`
steps.code:
export VAULT_ID="your-vault-uuid-here"

AGENT_RESPONSE=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"web-backend","token_ttl_seconds":900,"vault_ids":["'$VAULT_ID'"]}')

echo "$AGENT_RESPONSE"

steps.text: Extract the agent id and api_key from the response. The response looks like: {"agent":{"id":"7e3ce911-...","name":"web-backend",...},"api_key":"ocv_..."}. Save both values as env vars.
Exchange the agent credentials for a short-lived JWT. This endpoint needs no bearer token; the credentials in the body are the auth.
Confirm the token works by fetching the agent's own profile. You should see the ssh_public_key and ecdh_public_key fields.

blocks.text: You now have a registered agent and a fresh JWT bound to its vaults and TTL. Later calls use a Bearer JWT like this one; you will refresh it when policies change.

blocks.situation: A team is migrating a batch job to an agent identity. They ask whether to reuse the service account credential the job already has, since it is already scoped correctly.
blocks.question: What do you advise?

options.text: Reuse it. The scope is already right, and fewer credentials is better.
options.feedback: Fewer credentials is a real goal, but this shares one identity between a deterministic job and a principal that can be steered by its input. When something goes wrong, the audit trail cannot tell you which one did it.

options.text: Give the agent its own identity, because an agent is a different kind of principal and attribution must distinguish them.
options.feedback: Correct. Scope is only half of what an identity provides; the other half is answering who did this. An agent can be talked into acting, so its actions need to be separable from a job that cannot be.

options.text: Reuse it but add a header identifying which caller is which.
options.feedback: A caller-supplied header is not an identity. Anything that can set it can claim to be either party, which is precisely the property you need to not have.

options.text: Give the agent its own identity only if it will use the Intents API.
options.feedback: Signing raises the stakes but does not create the need. The attribution and blast-radius argument applies to a read-only agent too.

quiz.question: How many times is the plaintext ocv_ API key returned?
options: Once, at agent creation or key rotation
Once per day
On every token exchange
Never, it stays in the HSM
quiz.explanation: Only the argon2 hash is stored; the plaintext is shown once at creation or rotation.

quiz.question: Which endpoint turns an agent_id plus api_key into a JWT?
options: POST /v1/vaults
POST /v1/agents
GET /v1/agents/me
POST /v1/auth/agent-token
quiz.explanation: POST /v1/auth/agent-token takes agent_id and api_key in the body and returns a short-lived access_token. The long-lived key stays at rest and the short-lived token is what travels.

quiz.question: What two keypairs does 1Claw auto-generate for a new agent?
options: Ed25519 signing and P-256 ECDH
secp256k1 and Ed25519
Two AES keys
RSA and DSA
quiz.explanation: An Ed25519 signing keypair and a P-256 ECDH keypair, both stored in a dedicated __agent-keys vault. They exist so agent-to-agent messaging can be authenticated and encrypted without you provisioning anything.

concepts.note: the principal that can be talked into things

title: Policies and scoped access
summary: Grant an agent read access to one secret path, then use deny rules and priority to carve exceptions out of a broad grant.

blocks.text: A fresh agent has zero access. Its JWT carries an empty scope list until a human writes a policy. Policies tie a principal to path patterns and permissions, so you decide exactly what an agent can touch.

items: * matches one path segment
** matches zero or more segments (any depth)
read: GET a value and list metadata
write: PUT and DELETE at matching paths

blocks.text: When you create, update, or delete an agent's policy, all of that agent's active JWTs are revoked immediately. The agent must re-exchange its API key to pick up the new scope.

steps.text: Export your keys and IDs. Use the values saved from Lesson 1.
steps.code:
export ONECLAW_API_KEY="1ck_your_key_here"
export VAULT_ID="your-vault-uuid-here"
export AGENT_ID="your-agent-uuid-here"

steps.text: Create a policy that lets the agent read only api-keys/openai. The pattern is a single path, so the agent cannot reach anything else in the vault.
Re-exchange the agent key for a fresh JWT. The old token was revoked by the policy change.
Read the allowed path (works), then try a different path. Both 403 (forbidden) and 404 (not found) confirm the agent cannot access that path.

blocks.text: Policies also support runtime conditions: an IP allowlist (specific IPs or CIDR ranges) and a time window (allowed hours and days). Add these when an agent runs from known infrastructure.
Your agent can now read one secret path and nothing else, and any policy change takes effect on the very next request.
Policy Engine v2 (v0.47) added three fields that turn policies from a flat allow-list into a real evaluation model: effect, priority, and attribute_conditions.

items: effect: "allow" or "deny". A deny rule lets you punch a hole in a broad allow.
priority: an integer; higher wins when two policies both match the same path.
attribute_conditions: JSONB for fine-grained matching beyond path, IP, and time.

steps.text: Grant the agent broad read access across the vault.
Now carve out the one prefix it must never read, with a higher priority so it wins the overlap.
Verify. The first read succeeds, the second is denied by the higher-priority deny rule.
steps.code:
1claw secret get app/search/api-key   # allowed
1claw secret get app/billing/stripe   # denied

blocks.text: Priority decides overlaps, not effect. A deny rule does not automatically beat an allow: give it the higher priority, or the broad allow may win.

blocks.situation: An agent needs to read everything under app/ except the billing prefix. You write an allow on app/** with priority 10, and a deny on app/billing/** with priority 5. In testing the agent reads app/billing/stripe successfully.
blocks.question: What is wrong?

options.text: Deny rules only apply to human principals, not agents.
options.feedback: Effects apply to any principal. There is no distinction of that kind in the model, and believing there is would hide a much larger hole than this one.

options.text: The deny has a lower priority than the allow, so the allow wins the overlap.
options.feedback: Correct. Priority resolves overlaps and 10 beats 5. The intuition that deny automatically wins comes from other systems; here a deny rule with a lower number is silently inert, which is the dangerous part.

options.text: Glob patterns do not support a double asterisk, so app/billing/** never matched.
options.feedback: The pattern is fine and does match. If globbing were the problem the deny would fail on every path, not lose an overlap to a competing rule.

options.text: The agent's JWT was minted before the deny existed and had stale scopes.
options.feedback: A reasonable guess, since policy changes do revoke an agent's active tokens and force a re-exchange. But that would produce a stale-permissions failure, not a permanent one, and a fresh token here still reads the secret.

quiz.question: What access does an agent have before any policy is written?
options: Full read on all vaults
Read on its own vault only
Read plus write on the default vault
Zero access, empty scopes
quiz.explanation: Zero access with empty scopes. Creating an identity grants nothing on its own, which is why the public enrollment endpoint is not the open door it first appears to be.

quiz.question: In a policy pattern, what does ** match?
options: Only the vault root
Nothing: it is a literal
Exactly one segment
Zero or more segments at any depth
quiz.explanation: * matches one segment, ** matches zero or more at any depth. The difference decides whether app/* reaches app/billing/stripe, and getting it wrong widens a grant silently rather than erroring.

quiz.question: What happens to active JWTs when an agent's policy changes?
options: They are revoked immediately
They gain the new scope automatically
Nothing until they expire
Only write tokens are revoked
quiz.explanation: Any policy create, update, or delete revokes the agent's active JWTs so stale scopes cannot linger.

quiz.question: An allow policy on app/** has priority 10 and a deny policy on app/billing/** has priority 5. What happens on a read of app/billing/stripe?
options: Both policies are ignored
The read is allowed, because the allow rule has higher priority
The request errors as an unresolvable conflict
The read is denied, because deny always beats allow
quiz.explanation: Priority resolves the overlap, and 10 beats 5. Deny does not win automatically: the deny rule needs the higher priority number to take effect.

concepts.note: deny-by-default, and why priority decides overlaps

title: Lab: find out what your policy actually matches
summary: Write three patterns you believe are narrow, then list what each one really reaches.

blocks.text: The policy lesson gave you 1Claw's glob semantics: a single asterisk matches one segment and a double asterisk matches any depth. That is correct for 1Claw and it is not universal, and the gap between the semantics you assume and the ones your engine implements is where scope quietly widens.
This lab uses Python's fnmatch, which is what a naive implementation reaches for. Watch what it does with patterns that look obviously narrow.

steps.text: List the paths in a vault, then ask three patterns what they reach.
steps.code:
cat > /tmp/glob.py <<'EOF'
import fnmatch

PATHS = ["app/key", "app/billing/stripe", "app/billing/eu/vat",
         "apps/other/key", "app-staging/key"]

# how a naive implementation often handles ** : collapse it to *
naive = lambda pat, path: fnmatch.fnmatch(path, pat.replace("**", "*"))

print("intent: everything directly under app/, and NOT the billing subtree\n")
for pat in ["app/*", "app/**", "app*"]:
    hits = [p for p in PATHS if naive(pat, p)]
    print(f"  {pat:10} -> {hits}")
EOF
python3 /tmp/glob.py

steps.text: Three patterns, three surprises.
steps.code:
intent: everything directly under app/, and NOT the billing subtree

  app/*      -> ['app/key', 'app/billing/stripe', 'app/billing/eu/vat']
  app/**     -> ['app/key', 'app/billing/stripe', 'app/billing/eu/vat']
  app*       -> ['app/key', 'app/billing/stripe', 'app/billing/eu/vat', 'apps/other/key', 'app-staging/key']

steps.text: Clean up.

items: app/* reached two levels down, because fnmatch's asterisk crosses the separator. If you assumed shell behaviour, where an asterisk stops at a slash, you just granted the billing subtree.
app/** behaved identically, so under this implementation the two patterns you would use to mean different things mean the same thing.
app* reached apps/other/key and app-staging/key. A single missing slash walked out of the prefix entirely and into two sibling trees you did not know existed.

blocks.text: None of this contradicts what the policies lesson told you about 1Claw, where a single asterisk does stop at one segment. That is the point: the same pattern means different things in different engines, and a pattern you carry over from another system will not necessarily mean what it meant there.

The habit worth forming is small. Before relying on a pattern, list what it matches against the paths you actually have, including the ones you did not intend to include. A grant is defined by what it reaches, not by what you meant.

The third case is the one to watch for in review. Prefixes without a trailing separator are how a policy meant for app/ ends up covering app-staging/, and it reads as narrow at a glance because it is short.

quiz.question: Under fnmatch, why did app/* reach app/billing/stripe?
options: The path list was unsorted
The pattern was compiled incorrectly
fnmatch's asterisk crosses the path separator, unlike a shell glob
billing is a reserved prefix
quiz.explanation: Shell globbing stops an asterisk at a slash and fnmatch does not. Carrying the shell intuition into a policy written against fnmatch silently widens the grant by every level below.

quiz.question: What went wrong with app* specifically?
options: Without a trailing separator it matched sibling prefixes like apps/ and app-staging/
It excluded app/key
It only matched the first result
It required an anchor character
quiz.explanation: A missing slash turns a prefix into a substring match. It reads as narrow because it is short, which is what makes it easy to approve in review.

quiz.question: What does this lab imply about 1Claw's documented semantics?
options: fnmatch should be used for all policies
They are correct for 1Claw, and the lesson is that semantics differ between engines so patterns should be tested rather than assumed
Double asterisks should be avoided entirely
They are wrong; a single asterisk crosses segments
quiz.explanation: 1Claw's engine does stop a single asterisk at one segment. The transferable habit is listing what a pattern actually matches, because the same syntax means different things in different implementations.

title: Cedar and OPA policy backends
summary: Express authorization as declarative Cedar or Rego policy, and dry-run it before it ever denies a real request.

blocks.text: Path patterns and conditions cover most access control. When rules get genuinely complex (cross-resource logic, org-specific data lookups), 1Claw supports two declarative policy backends alongside the built-in engine.

items: Cedar (Team tier and above): AWS's authorization language. Principal, action, resource, context.
OPA (Business tier and above): Open Policy Agent, using Rego and custom data documents.
Both are additive. The built-in policy engine still runs; these express rules it cannot.

blocks.text: Both backends ship a test endpoint that evaluates a policy against a hypothetical request without saving it. Use it before you create anything.

steps.text: Write a Cedar policy. This one forbids any agent from reading production secrets outside business hours.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/org/cedar-policies \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "no-prod-reads-after-hours",
    "policy": "forbid(principal in Group::\"agents\", action == Action::\"read\", resource in Vault::\"production\") when { context.hour > 18 };"
  }'

steps.text: Dry-run it before trusting it. Supply a principal, action, resource, and context and see the decision.
List what is active, from the CLI.
The OPA equivalent takes Rego plus an input document.

blocks.text: Cedar is Team+ and OPA is Business+. On a lower tier these endpoints exist but return a tier error, so check your plan before designing around them.

You rarely write Cedar by hand for a first agent. Policy presets (Team+ for the Cedar export) answer a plainer question instead: read-only-assistant, small-business-spender, inbox-agent, treasury-operator, each a sentence that compiles to the same guardrail columns, access policies and approval rules you would otherwise write by hand.

Preview before you apply. POST /v1/agents/{id}/policy-preset/preview returns exactly which fields the preset would widen relative to what the agent can already do, so "this raises your daily limit from $10 to $100" is what a human reads, not a generic warning.

A preset is not a way around approval. Applying one that loosens a guardrail returns 202 or 403, never a silent 200, because a preset builds the same request a person editing the agent by hand would send and passes it to the same handler: same widening classification, same approval queue, same step-up. A wizard that wrote guardrail columns directly would be a way around that flow wearing a friendlier interface.

The Cedar export makes the same discipline visible in the generated policy itself. Presets state limits in dollars; Cedar's schema only exposes transaction value as value_gwei, a native-token amount. Converting needs a live price, and a price baked into a policy at write time is wrong the moment it is written and stays silently wrong from then on.

So the compiler does not convert. USD limits come back separately as residual_guardrails and stay enforced by the guardrail columns, where a live price applies at evaluation time. Render residual_guardrails next to the Cedar text: a generated policy shown alone reads as complete while actually permitting every amount, the same silent gap a decimal-place error leaves in a transaction value.

Policies created from a Cedar export start in shadow mode, the same enforcement: log setting taught earlier in this course, reporting what they would decide without deciding anything until someone promotes them. Dry-run one with the same test endpoint you already used above before promoting it.

blocks.situation: You have written a Cedar policy that forbids agents from reading production secrets outside business hours. It is your first Cedar policy and production traffic runs continuously.
blocks.question: How do you roll it out?

options.text: Create it and watch the audit log for unexpected denials.
options.feedback: This is a test in production with real denials as the signal. If the policy is wrong you find out from a failed job at 02:00, which is both the worst time to learn it and the worst way.

options.text: Dry-run it against representative principals and contexts with the test endpoint, then create it.
options.feedback: Correct. The test endpoint evaluates a full principal, action, resource and context and returns the decision without saving anything, so you can confirm the boundary conditions before any request is affected.

options.text: Create it with a short expiry so it lapses if it turns out to be wrong.
options.feedback: Expiry limits how long a mistake lasts but does nothing about the damage inside the window, and a policy that silently lapses is its own failure mode.

options.text: Deploy it to a sub-organization first as a staging environment.
options.feedback: Sub-orgs isolate resources, not policy semantics, and a sub-org without production traffic will not exercise the time conditions you are actually unsure about.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the /v1/org/cedar-policies/test endpoint?
options: Apply the policy to every past request
Verify the policy's syntax only
Load-test the policy engine
Dry-run a policy against a hypothetical request without saving it
quiz.explanation: The test endpoint evaluates a full principal/action/resource/context request and returns the decision, so you can confirm behaviour before a policy affects live traffic.

quiz.question: How do Cedar and OPA policies relate to the built-in policy engine?
options: They only apply to human users
They only apply to on-chain signing
They are additive: the built-in engine still runs
They replace the built-in engine entirely
quiz.explanation: Both are additional backends layered alongside the built-in engine, for rules that path patterns and conditions cannot express.

quiz.question: Which tiers gate Cedar and OPA respectively?
options: Both are Free
Both are Enterprise-only
Cedar is Business+, OPA is Team+
Cedar is Team+, OPA is Business+
quiz.explanation: Cedar requires Team or above; OPA requires Business or above. On lower tiers the endpoints return a tier error.

quiz.question: A Cedar export from a policy preset comes back with residual_guardrails listing a $5000 daily cap. Why doesn't that cap appear as a value_gwei condition inside the Cedar text itself?
options: Cedar does not support numeric comparisons
Converting a USD limit to a native-token amount needs a live price, and a price baked into the policy at write time would be silently wrong from that moment on
residual_guardrails is a display-only field with no real enforcement behind it
Dollar limits only apply to human-authored policies, not generated ones
quiz.explanation: The compiler deliberately does not convert. The dollar limit stays enforced by the guardrail columns, where a live price is applied at evaluation time, and is repeated in residual_guardrails so a reader does not mistake the Cedar text alone for the complete policy.

title: Agent self-enrollment and approvals
summary: Let an agent enroll itself with no credentials and route the approval to a human.

blocks.text: This creates a new agent via self-enrollment: a different bootstrap path from Lesson 1's human-initiated registration. Sometimes the agent boots before anyone has provisioned it. The enroll endpoint is public, so an agent can request its own identity and wait for a human to approve. The API key is emailed to the human after approval and never returned to the agent.
Two enrollment methods follow. Pick one: the email path suits a human who is not at their terminal, and the approval-URL path suits one who is.

steps.text: Option A: Submit an enrollment with a name and a human_email. Allow and Deny links are sent to that address. No credentials are required.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/enroll \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"deploy-bot","human_email":"alice@example.com","description":"CI pipeline agent"}'

steps.text: Option B: Send name only. The response includes an enrollment_id and an approval_url the human opens while signed in. No email needed. Sample response: {"enrollment_id":"enr_abc123","approval_url":"https://1claw.co/approve/enr_abc123","status":"pending"}
The human approves via the emailed link or the approval_url. After approval an agent is created in their org and the ocv_ key is emailed to them.
The human then writes a policy so the new agent can read the paths it needs. Follow Lesson 2 (Policies and scoped access) in this track.

blocks.text: For sensitive actions an agent can also file an approval with POST /v1/approvals/request, directed to its creator. Requests carry a risk tier: T1 is informational, T2 requires biometric step-up, and T3 requires passkey plus TOTP attestation before the human can approve.
Enrollment is rate limited: one per email per 10 minutes when email is used, plus caps on pending rows and per-IP limits. Some branches return a uniform 201 to limit email enumeration.
You can now bootstrap an agent from zero credentials and hand the approval to a human, who receives the key and grants scoped access.

blocks.situation: Self-enrollment is public: an agent posts a name and a human's email, and credentials are mailed to that human. A security reviewer flags this as an open registration endpoint and asks you to remove it.
blocks.question: How do you answer?

options.text: They are right; remove it and provision agents only from the dashboard.
options.feedback: It closes a door that was not open. Enrollment creates an identity with zero access until a human writes a policy, so the endpoint grants nothing on its own.

options.text: Enrollment creates an identity with no access until a human grants it, and it is rate limited per email and per IP, so the open endpoint is not the risk it appears to be.
options.feedback: Correct. The reviewer is applying a sound instinct to the wrong shape. What matters is not who can create an identity but what an identity can do on creation, and the answer here is nothing.

options.text: It is fine because the credentials go to the human, who must be a real 1Claw user.
options.feedback: True and worth saying, but on its own it argues that delivery is safe rather than that creation is harmless. The zero-access default is the load-bearing part.

options.text: Add an allowlist of domains permitted to enroll.
options.feedback: A reasonable hardening if you want it, but proposing a control before establishing whether there is a risk concedes the reviewer's premise.

quiz.question: Where does the enrolled agent's API key go?
options: Printed to the server log
Emailed to the human after approval
Stored in the agent's env
Returned in the enroll response
quiz.explanation: The plaintext key is emailed to the approving human and is never returned from the enroll endpoint.

quiz.question: Which risk tier requires passkey plus TOTP attestation?
options: T3
T2
T1
None require step-up
quiz.explanation: T3 requires passkey plus TOTP. The tiers exist so that low-value approvals stay cheap: making every decision require the strongest factor produces reflexive approval, which is worse than a weaker factor used attentively.

quiz.question: What can an agent submit with name only and no email?
options: A link-only enrollment returning an approval_url
A policy change
Nothing, email is mandatory
A full agent with an immediate key
quiz.explanation: Name-only enrollment creates a link-only pending enrollment and returns an approval_url for a signed-in human.

concepts.note: zero access until a human grants it

title: MCP server integration
summary: Connect an AI client to the 1Claw MCP server and run a first list_secrets call.

blocks.text: The 1Claw MCP server gives an AI client just-in-time access to vault secrets over the Model Context Protocol. It exposes 141 tools (vault, Intents signing, Execution Intents bindings, treasury, approvals, automations, runtimes, memory, chat, channels, Cedar/OPA policy backends, and Safe agent accounts). The canonical setup is local stdio: `npx @1claw/mcp` with a single ONECLAW_AGENT_API_KEY env var; the server exchanges it for a JWT, refreshes before expiry, and auto-discovers the agent and vault. The MCP server itself enforces nothing: every call is checked against the agent's policies by the vault API.
Requires: 1Claw account, a vault with secrets, an agent, and a read policy (see Lessons 1-2).

steps.text: Recommended: local stdio. Run the server as a process and pass only the agent API key. It exchanges the key for a JWT, auto-refreshes it, and auto-discovers the agent and vault: no agent_id, no vault ID, no manual token minting. Paste this into .cursor/mcp.json, claude_desktop_config.json, or any MCP client that supports stdio.
Mint an agent JWT. Use env vars from Lesson 1 or paste your agent_id and ocv_ key directly.
steps.code:
export ONECLAW_AGENT_ID="your-agent-uuid"
export ONECLAW_AGENT_KEY="ocv_your_agent_api_key"
export VAULT_ID="your-vault-uuid"

TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/auth/agent-token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"agent_id":"'$ONECLAW_AGENT_ID'","api_key":"'$ONECLAW_AGENT_KEY'"}' | jq -r .access_token)

steps.text: Alternative: hosted server. Only for non-IDE callers that can mint a fresh JWT per connection (the token from the previous step). Paste your $TOKEN and $VAULT_ID into the headers.
Restart the client and ask it to list your secrets. The agent calls list_secrets and returns paths and metadata, never values.
steps.code: List the secrets in my 1claw vault.

blocks.text: Do not point an IDE at the hosted https://mcp.1claw.co/mcp URL with a static Bearer token. Agent JWTs expire in about 15 minutes by default, so the connection dies mid-session and the client will not re-mint it. Use the stdio server for Cursor, Claude Desktop, VS Code, and Claude Code; it refreshes the token for you.
Output inspection runs by default. If a known secret value ever appears in a non-secret tool's output, it is replaced with [REDACTED:#hashprefix] before it reaches the model context.
Your AI client is now wired to the vault, and a first list_secrets call returns metadata scoped to the agent's policies.

blocks.situation: A developer installs a third-party MCP server alongside 1Claw in their editor. It is open source, has plenty of stars, and its tool descriptions are unusually detailed and helpful.
blocks.question: What is the risk that is easy to miss?

options.text: It could exfiltrate secrets by calling the 1Claw tools directly.
options.feedback: MCP servers do not call each other's tools; the client does. A malicious server influences the model rather than invoking your vault itself.

options.text: Tool descriptions are read by the model as guidance, so unusually detailed text is an injection surface as much as the server's code.
options.feedback: Correct, and it is why the detail is worth noticing rather than appreciating. Descriptions enter the context window and can carry instructions, which makes an installed tool's metadata part of your attack surface.

options.text: It might consume enough context tokens to crowd out the 1Claw tools.
options.feedback: A genuine annoyance and a cost concern, but it degrades usefulness rather than creating an exposure.

options.text: It could impersonate the 1Claw server and capture the agent key.
options.feedback: The stdio server receives its key from the client's own config, so another server has no path to it. Worth pinning versions regardless, but this is not the mechanism.

quiz.question: Which two headers authenticate a hosted MCP connection?
options: Cookie and X-Vault-ID
Authorization and X-Client-Share
Authorization and X-Vault-ID
X-Api-Key and X-Agent-ID
quiz.explanation: The hosted server takes a Bearer JWT in Authorization and the vault UUID in X-Vault-ID.

quiz.question: Who enforces access control for MCP tool calls?
options: The LLM provider
The AI client
The MCP server itself
The vault API policy engine
quiz.explanation: The MCP server just relays requests; the vault API checks every call against the agent's policies.

quiz.question: What does list_secrets return?
options: Decrypted values
Only the vault name
Paths, types, versions, and metadata only
The agent's private keys
quiz.explanation: Metadata only: paths, types and versions, never values. That split is what lets an agent discover what exists without being able to read it, and get_secret is separately policy-checked.

concepts.note: why tool descriptions are untrusted input

title: Execution Intents and bindings
summary: Let an agent call an external API through a binding, so the credential is injected server-side and never enters the model's context.

blocks.text: Policies control which secrets an agent can read. Execution Intents go further: the agent never reads the credential at all. You pre-configure a binding that holds the credential server-side, and the agent asks 1Claw to perform the call on its behalf.

items: The agent sends an intent (method, path, body), not a key.
1Claw injects the credential, applies host and path allowlists, and makes the request.
The response comes back to the agent. The secret was never in its context window.
Revoking a binding cuts access instantly, with no secret to rotate.

blocks.text: This is the pattern 1claw.co leads with on its own homepage: credentials stay server-side and agents execute through bindings.

steps.text: Create an HTTP binding holding a Stripe key. The credential is stored server-side against the binding.
Prefer a live pointer over a copied credential. With credential_source vault_ref the value is resolved from the vault at execution time, so rotating the secret needs no binding update.
Test the binding before an agent depends on it. The binding subcommands take the agent id and the binding id as positional arguments, so list them first to get the id.
steps.code:
1claw agent binding list $AGENT_ID
1claw agent binding test $AGENT_ID $BINDING_ID

steps.text: Execute through it. This is what the agent calls: note there is no credential anywhere in the request.
From the SDK, the same call reads the way the homepage example does.

blocks.text: Binding types beyond HTTP: GraphQL (Pro), plus Postgres, MySQL, Redis, gRPC, SMTP, Cloud SDK, S3 and Custom on Team and above. Business+ can run execution inside the TEE with execution_surface set to tee.

Set execution_require_tee on the agent to force every execution through Shroud AND block the agent's direct secret reads outright. It is the strongest form of this pattern, but it requires execution_intents_enabled first.

The Stripe binding above was hand-configured: base URL, allowed hosts, allowed paths, all chosen by you. Connectors are the same binding for common providers with those three decisions already made. Installing Gmail, Slack, GitHub, Notion or Discord is one call instead of four, but the interesting part is what that call refuses to let you skip.

items: The binding a connector install creates is scoped to that connector: gmail reaches gmail.googleapis.com/gmail/v1/ and nothing else, the same allowed_hosts and allowed_paths discipline you just configured by hand for Stripe.

That is the actual difference from a bare OAuth connection. An HTTP binding with no allowed_hosts has no host restriction, so a binding holding a user's Google token could be pointed anywhere; a connector's cannot.
Requested scopes may narrow a preset's list and may not extend it. A scope outside the preset is a 400, and so is dropping one the preset marks required.

Installed is not connected. A 201 means the binding exists; it holds no credential until the human finishes the OAuth round trip, and GET /v1/agents/{id}/connectors reports connected separately from installed.

blocks.text: Installing a connector is human-only, the same rule as everything else in this lesson with a high blast radius. An agent calling the install endpoint for itself gets a 403: giving an agent reach into a third-party account starts a flow that runs in a person's browser, not an agent's context.

blocks.situation: A binding holds a partner API key inline. The partner rotates the credential on a schedule, and every rotation breaks your agent until someone updates the binding by hand. A colleague proposes storing the key in the vault and giving the agent read access to that path, so it can fetch the current value before each call.
blocks.question: What do you do?

options.text: Take the proposal. Reading from the vault is the same trust boundary as the binding.
options.feedback: It is not. The moment the agent reads that value it is in the model's context, which is exactly what Execution Intents exists to prevent. The proposal solves the rotation problem by giving up the property that made bindings worth using.

options.text: Change the binding's credential_source to a vault_ref pointing at that path.
options.feedback: Correct. The credential is resolved server-side at execution time, so rotation is picked up automatically and the agent still never sees the value. It solves the same problem as the proposal without moving the secret into context.

options.text: Keep the inline credential and add a scheduled automation to update the binding after each rotation.
options.feedback: This works and is a real option, but it is machinery to keep two copies in sync when the platform can hold one. It also leaves a window after each rotation where the binding is stale.

options.text: Rotate the binding credential through the rotate-credential endpoint on a timer.
options.feedback: That endpoint changes the stored credential to a value you supply; it does not discover the partner's new key. You would still need to fetch the new value from somewhere, which returns you to the original problem.

quiz.question: What is the main security advantage of executing through a binding rather than reading the secret?
options: The request is faster
The credential is injected server-side and never enters the agent's context
The agent gets a longer-lived token
The credential is rotated after every call
quiz.explanation: The agent sends an intent, not a key. The credential stays server-side, so it cannot leak into the context window, logs, or model memory.

quiz.question: Why choose credential_source vault_ref over an inline credential?
options: The credential resolves from the vault at execution time, so rotation needs no binding update
It removes the need for allowed_hosts
It encrypts the credential more strongly
It makes the binding usable by every agent
quiz.explanation: Inline copies the credential at creation. A vault_ref is a live pointer resolved at execution, so rotating the underlying secret is picked up automatically.

quiz.question: What does execution_require_tee do beyond forcing execution through Shroud?
options: It grants the agent Business tier features
It exempts the agent from binding allowlists
It disables the agent's signing keys
It also blocks the agent's direct secret reads
quiz.explanation: It forces execution through the TEE and blocks direct secret reads by that agent, pushing it entirely onto bindings. It requires execution_intents_enabled to be on first.

quiz.question: You install the Gmail connector and request only the readonly scope, narrower than the preset's default list. What happens if you then try to widen it to a scope outside the preset entirely?
options: It succeeds, since you already proved you can narrow the request
It returns 400. Requested scopes may narrow a preset's list but never extend it
It silently falls back to the preset's default scopes
It succeeds only on Business tier and above
quiz.explanation: The reviewed scope list is what makes a one-click install different from a general OAuth initiator. Narrowing is always allowed; asking for anything the preset does not already cover is a 400.

concepts.note: keeping the credential out of context

title: Lab: build a credential broker
summary: Write both patterns side by side, dump each agent's context, and see the difference the broker makes.

blocks.text: Execution Intents is a small idea with a large consequence, and the fastest way to believe it is to implement both sides. Forty lines of Python, no network, no account. The question the lab answers is narrow and concrete: after the agent has done its job, is the credential in its context?

steps.text: Write both agents. The first reads the credential the obvious way; the second sends an intent and lets a broker do the call.
Read the two context dumps. They are the whole lesson.
steps.code:
ReadingAgent:
    fetched credential: sk-live-9f2a
    calling stripe with sk-live-9f2a
  -> credential in context: YES

BrokeredAgent:
    intent: stripe GET /v1/balance
    result: balance: 42.00
  -> credential in context: no

an injected agent tries something else:
    DENIED: stripe POST /v1/transfers is not an allowed intent

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: Both agents got the same answer. Only one of them is a problem if it is later asked to repeat everything it knows.

items: The reading agent's context contains a live credential. A prompt injection at any later turn can ask for it, and any log, trace or provider request that captured the context has it too.
The brokered agent's context contains an intent and a result. There is nothing to exfiltrate because there was never anything to hold.
The last line is the second property, and it is easy to miss. The broker refused an intent it was not configured for, so a successfully injected agent still could not initiate a transfer.

blocks.text: Notice that the broker is trivial: an allowlist, a lookup, and a call. The security value is not in its sophistication, it is in where it sits. The check runs somewhere the agent's context cannot reach and cannot argue with.

This is the shape of Execution Intents. A binding is the allowlist plus the stored credential, credential_source with a vault_ref is the lookup resolved at execution time, and the agent sends the same kind of intent your BrokeredAgent sent. The production version adds host and path guardrails, credential rotation, per-binding limits and an audit trail, and the property it protects is the one you just demonstrated in forty lines.

The broker still holds the credential, so this shrinks the private-data circle rather than removing it. An attacker who compromises the broker gets everything, which is why the real implementation keeps that material in an HSM and constrains what a binding may call.

quiz.question: After both agents complete, what is the difference in their contexts?
options: Neither holds anything sensitive
The brokered agent holds a hashed credential
The reading agent holds a live credential; the brokered one holds only an intent and a result
Both hold the credential, but the brokered one encrypts it
quiz.explanation: That difference is the entire point. There is nothing to exfiltrate from the brokered agent because it never received the value.

quiz.question: What did the DENIED line demonstrate?
options: The broker rate-limits requests
A successfully injected agent still cannot initiate an action the broker was not configured for
POST requests are never allowed
The credential had expired
quiz.explanation: Brokering provides two properties, not one: the credential stays out of context, and the set of possible actions is bounded by the allowlist rather than by the agent's judgment.

quiz.question: What does brokering not solve?
options: Auditing which agent called what
Limiting request rates
Credential rotation
The broker still holds the credential, so compromising it yields everything
quiz.explanation: It shrinks the private-data circle rather than removing it, which is why production implementations keep the material in an HSM and constrain what each binding may reach.

title: Agent-to-human sharing
summary: Let an agent hand a credential it discovered or generated back to the human who created it, without knowing their email.

blocks.text: Sharing usually runs human to human. The reverse direction matters for autonomous work: an agent provisions a resource, gets a credential, and needs to hand it to a person. It should not need to know who that person is.
Setting recipient_type to "creator" solves this. The API resolves the recipient from the agent's own created_by field: no email, no user ID, nothing the agent could get wrong or leak.
Requires: an agent with write access to a vault, from the earlier lessons in this track.
recipient_type accepts user, agent, external_email, anyone_with_link, or creator. Only creator resolves the recipient from the agent's own created_by field.

steps.text: As the agent, share the secret back to its creator. Shares are addressed by secret ID, and expires_at is required.
As the human, list what is waiting in the Inbound tab.
Accept it. Until you do, the share is pending and grants nothing.

blocks.text: This is the clean pattern for agents that generate credentials: the agent creates the value, shares it to its creator, and the human accepts. The agent never needs directory access or an email address.

blocks.situation: An agent provisions a database and needs to hand the generated password to the human who created it. A developer proposes having the agent look up that human's email from the org directory and share to it.
blocks.question: What is wrong with the proposal?

options.text: Nothing, provided the agent has directory read access.
options.feedback: Granting directory access to solve this is the problem. You have widened the agent's reach to every user's contact details in order to avoid a field the API already resolves for you.

options.text: It needs directory access it should not have, when recipient_type creator resolves the recipient from created_by server-side.
options.feedback: Correct. The agent never needs to know or store who its human is. Removing the lookup removes both a failure mode and a small standing data exposure.

options.text: Email-based shares are less secure than user-id shares.
options.feedback: Both are legitimate recipient types with the same acceptance step. The issue is what the agent had to be granted to determine the address.

options.text: The agent cannot share secrets at all; sharing is human-only.
options.feedback: Agents can share, and sharing back to their creator is a supported pattern. The design question is how the recipient gets resolved.

quiz.question: Why use recipient_type "creator" instead of the human's email?
options: It skips the acceptance step
The API resolves the recipient from the agent's created_by field, so the agent needs no identity data
It grants write access automatically
It delivers the share faster
quiz.explanation: The agent does not need to know or store who its human is. The server resolves it from created_by, which removes both a failure mode and a small data-leak surface.

quiz.question: What happens to a share before the human accepts it?
options: It is pending and grants nothing
It expires after one minute
It is auto-accepted for the creator
The recipient already has full access
quiz.explanation: Shares are pending until accepted. The recipient sees it in their Inbound tab and must accept before any access is granted.

title: Peer memory: access control for what nobody granted
summary: Several agents can share a model of one human. That model is derived, not granted, which changes what access control has to mean.

blocks.text: Everything so far in this track has been about access to something a human explicitly created or owns: a secret, a vault, a delegation. Peer memory is different in kind. When several agents serve the same person, each one that learns their approval habits independently learns less than the group could learn together. A peer is that shared model: what a person has approved, how confidently, and why the system believes it.

It is also the most sensitive thing an agent can read about someone, and unlike a secret, nobody deliberately granted it. A password exists because a human typed it in. A behavioral profile exists because the system noticed a pattern. That difference is why the access model here is stricter than anything else in this track, not looser.

items: An agent may read or write a peer only if it is named in observer_agent_ids, full stop.
Same organization grants nothing. Same platform connection grants nothing. A broad scope grants nothing.
A peer with no observers is readable by no agent at all, not by every agent.
Creating a peer, which decides who observes it, is human-only. An agent that could create one could add itself as an observer.

blocks.text: That third point is deliberate, not an oversight. If an empty observer list meant "everyone", forgetting to set observers would expose someone's behavioral profile to every agent in the org, silently and totally. Empty means nobody, the same deny-by-default default this course has taught since Access Control Models.

What actually gets derived is narrower than it sounds. The system tracks approval tendencies, and only from a consistent history: per fingerprint bucket (action, amount band, new-or-known recipient), never per action type in general, so three approvals of $5 do not become a belief that spans $500. Three observations minimum: two is a coincidence. A mixed history, someone who sometimes says no, is not recorded as a tendency at all, because deciding case by case is the opposite of a pattern worth automating. And confidence is capped below certainty; a score of 1.0 would read downstream as "no need to check", which is never true.

POST /v1/peers/{id}/predict-approval returns likelihood (an observation about the person) and suggest_auto (a statement about your own action_approval_policy) as two separate fields. suggest_auto is true only where a rule you already wrote would auto-approve this exact case, and it carries a blocked_reason when it is not.

That separation is the whole point. A confident model of a person never becomes new authority by itself. If you never wrote a rule for this action, no_matching_rule comes back regardless of how many times the person has said yes before. An absent rule is not permission, the same principle behind deny-by-default policy engines, applied to a prediction instead of a request.

Every derived fact carries provenance, naming the events it came from. When those events pass the 90-day retention window, each entry becomes a tombstone: it keeps the kind of event and the decision, and drops the content. The belief outlives its transcript without losing its basis, so "why does this system think that about me" stays answerable years later. A human correction always outranks a re-derived inference; editing a fact stops the processor from overwriting it, because a correction that inference silently reverses is not a correction.

blocks.situation: Two of your agents serve the same customer-support user: a triage bot and a refund bot. The refund bot's policy auto-approves refunds under $20 for a peer with a strong approval history. The triage bot calls predict-approval on that peer to decide whether to fast-track a $15 refund request it received.
blocks.question: What does the triage bot's call return, and why?

options.text: suggest_auto: true, because the peer has a strong approval history for refunds.
options.feedback: Likelihood is about the person; suggest_auto is about the calling agent's own policy. The peer's history does not change what the triage bot is itself configured to do.

options.text: suggest_auto: false with blocked_reason no_matching_rule, because the rule that would auto-approve this lives on the refund bot's policy, not the triage bot's.
options.feedback: Correct. predict-approval consults the calling agent's own action_approval_policy. A rule on the refund bot does not transfer to the triage bot just because they observe the same peer. Authority does not travel with the data.

options.text: The call fails, because only one agent can observe a given peer at a time.
options.feedback: Multiple agents can be named in observer_agent_ids simultaneously; that is the entire point of a shared peer model. The call succeeds and returns a prediction.

options.text: suggest_auto: true, because $15 is under the refund bot's $20 threshold.
options.feedback: The $20 threshold belongs to the refund bot's policy, which the triage bot is not evaluated against. Each agent's suggest_auto reflects only its own rules.

blocks.text: Platform connections provision a peer automatically on bootstrap, with that connection's agents as observers, and re-running bootstrap merges observers rather than replacing them, so adding a new agent to a connection does not revoke the ones already watching. MCP exposes only get_peer_context to agents; creating a peer and changing its observer list have no MCP tool and stay human actions, the same pattern this course has taught for every action with a high blast radius.

quiz.question: An agent is in the same organization as a peer but not named in its observer_agent_ids. What can it read?
options: Nothing. Organization membership grants no access to a peer.
Everything, since organization membership is sufficient.
Only the peer's tombstoned facts, not live ones.
The peer's context, but not individual facts.
quiz.explanation: Access to a peer is by observer list and nothing else. Same org, same connection, and broad scopes all grant nothing on their own.

quiz.question: Why does an empty observer_agent_ids list mean "no agent may read this peer" rather than "every agent may"?
options: Because empty lists are rejected by the API and cannot be created.
Because if empty meant everyone, forgetting to set observers would silently expose a behavioral profile org-wide.
Because peers with no observers are deleted automatically after 90 days.
Both interpretations are supported, chosen by a per-org setting.
quiz.explanation: This is the same deny-by-default logic as an unscoped policy: an omission should fail closed, not open. A missing observer list must never be read as a wildcard.

quiz.question: predict-approval returns likelihood: 0.9 and suggest_auto: false with blocked_reason: no_matching_rule. What does this mean?
options: The prediction is unreliable and should be ignored.
The person is very likely to approve, but the calling agent has no rule that would auto-approve this case, so nothing is authorized.
The peer's data has expired past the retention window.
The agent is not permitted to observe this peer.
quiz.explanation: likelihood is an observation about the person. suggest_auto is a statement about the calling agent's own policy. A confident model never becomes new authority by itself; an absent rule is not permission.

quiz.question: A fact's supporting event passes the 90-day retention window. What happens to the fact?
options: It is deleted along with the event.
It becomes a tombstone: the kind of event and the decision remain, the content does not.
It is silently re-derived from newer events with the same content.
It is frozen and can never be corrected again.
quiz.explanation: The belief outlives its transcript without losing its basis. A tombstone keeps enough to answer "why does the system think that" without holding onto expired event content.

concepts.note: deny-by-default applied to derived, not granted, data
a confident prediction is not authority to act on

title: Sub-agents and delegation
summary: Let one agent hand work to another under a human-authored delegation, with tool allowlists, depth limits, and daily caps.

blocks.text: Agents can delegate tasks to other agents. The authorization for that is never something the agents arrange between themselves: a human creates an explicit delegation record, and agents cannot create, modify, or revoke their own (403).

items: allowed_tools / blocked_tools: exactly which tools the delegate may use.
max_daily_delegations: a rate limit counted from real invocations.
max_depth (1-10): stops recursive chains of agents calling agents.
delegation_mode: caller (delegate uses its own credentials, the default), target (uses the target agent's config), or both.
expires_at: delegations can be temporary.

blocks.text: Self-delegation is blocked with a 400, and an agent in one org can never delegate to an agent in another.

steps.text: As a human, authorize agent A to delegate to agent B, limited to two tools and ten calls a day.
The delegating agent discovers what it is actually allowed to do at runtime.
Delegate a task. The X-Delegation-Depth header is tracked and enforced against max_depth.
steps.code:
1claw agent delegation list
# via MCP the agent calls: delegate_task

steps.text: Revoke it. Human-only, effective immediately, and it takes both the delegating agent's id and the delegation id.

blocks.text: Every delegation emits audit events: agent.delegation.created, .updated, .revoked, .invoked, and .blocked. A blocked event is the one to alert on; it means an agent tried something outside its grant.

blocks.situation: A research agent delegates summarisation to a second agent. The delegation is human-created, scoped to two tools, and rate limited. The research agent reads public web pages; the summariser has vault access to internal notes.
blocks.question: Where is the exposure?

options.text: Nowhere. The delegation is explicit, scoped, and rate limited, which is the documented pattern.
options.feedback: Every one of those controls is correct and none of them addresses the actual path. Authorization decides that the summariser may be asked; it says nothing about what it is asked to do.

options.text: The summariser should treat the delegated task as untrusted content, because it can carry an injection from the web pages the caller read.
options.feedback: Correct. The research agent's input is attacker-influenced, so the task text it forwards is too. Authorization and content trust are independent, and a correctly scoped delegation still carries whatever was in the caller's context.

options.text: The rate limit is too high, letting an attacker exhaust the daily delegation budget.
options.feedback: Availability is worth bounding and the limit does that, but exhausting a quota is a denial of service. The exposure here is that internal notes can be summarised into an attacker-chosen shape and returned.

options.text: Delegation depth is unbounded, so the summariser could delegate onward indefinitely.
options.feedback: Worth checking, and max_depth exists for exactly that. But depth limits runaway chains; it does not stop the first hop from carrying a payload.

quiz.question: Who can create a delegation between two agents?
options: Either agent involved
A human: agents get a 403 creating their own
The delegating agent only
Any agent in the org
quiz.explanation: Delegation records are human-authored. Agents cannot create, modify, or revoke their own delegations; those calls return 403.

quiz.question: What does max_depth protect against?
options: Too many tools being allowed
Recursive chains of agents delegating onward indefinitely
Delegations lasting too long
Cross-organization delegation
quiz.explanation: Depth is tracked with the X-Delegation-Depth header and capped at max_depth (1-10), which stops A→B→C→… chains from running away.

quiz.question: In the default "caller" delegation mode, whose credentials does the delegate use?
options: Its own
A temporary shared credential
The delegating agent's
The human creator's
quiz.explanation: In caller mode the delegate acts with its own credentials and its own scopes. target mode instead runs it with the target agent's config and tools.

title: Lab: watch a delegation chain run away
summary: Let agents delegate onward and see what the depth limit is actually stopping.

blocks.text: The delegation lesson listed max_depth among the controls without saying much about what a runaway chain costs. Twenty lines make the failure legible.

steps.text: Model delegation records and a depth counter carried along the chain.
Every hop was individually authorised. The third was refused for how far it was from the original request.
steps.code:
a asks b, which asks c, which asks d:
  a->b ok at depth 1
  b->c ok at depth 2
  c->d DENIED (depth 3 over max_depth 2)

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: Notice what the limit is not doing. Every delegation in that chain was created by a human and every hop was permitted, so this is not catching an unauthorised call. It is bounding how far an instruction can travel from whoever originally made it.

items: Each hop carries the previous agent's context forward, so text that entered at a is being acted on at d, three interpretations later.
Accountability thins with distance. At depth three the question of who asked for this has three plausible answers and no single owner.
Without a limit the chain is bounded only by the delegation graph, and a cycle in that graph is unbounded.

blocks.text: The X-Delegation-Depth header is what carries the count, which means it has to be propagated. An agent implementation that forgets to forward it resets the depth to zero at every hop and turns the limit off without anything appearing to fail.

Two hops is enough for most legitimate designs. If you find yourself needing five, the shape of the problem is usually wrong: a coordinator calling three specialists directly is easier to reason about than a chain that passes the task along.

quiz.question: What is max_depth actually preventing?
options: Unauthorised delegations
Concurrent delegations
Too many agents in one organisation
How far an instruction can travel from whoever originally made it
quiz.explanation: Every hop in the chain was authorised. The limit bounds distance from the original request, which is where accountability and context integrity degrade.

quiz.question: What happens if an implementation forgets to forward X-Delegation-Depth?
options: The delegation record is invalidated
The request is rejected
The depth resets to zero at every hop, disabling the limit while nothing appears to fail
The chain is capped at one hop
quiz.explanation: The count is carried in the header. Losing it silently removes the control, which is the most dangerous kind of failure because nothing errors.

quiz.question: What does each hop carry with it?
options: Only the task description
A fresh, empty context
The previous agent's context, so text that entered at the first hop is acted on several interpretations later
The original user's credentials
quiz.explanation: That is why an injection at the start of a chain is worse than one at the end: it gets re-interpreted at every subsequent hop.

title: Agent discovery and A2A
summary: Publish an agent card to the public directory so other agents can find it over A2A and MCP.

blocks.text: Agent Discovery turns a private agent into something other agents can find. An agent card advertises what it does, which protocols it speaks, and where to reach it: A2A URL, MCP endpoint, categories, and pricing.
Discovery is opt-in and human-controlled. PATCH /v1/agents/{id}/discovery is human-only; an agent cannot publish itself.

steps.text: Publish the agent with a capability card.
steps.code:
curl -s -X PATCH https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AGENT_ID/discovery \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "discoverable": true,
    "categories": ["research", "data"],
    "description": "Summarizes on-chain activity for a given address.",
    "protocols": ["a2a", "mcp"]
  }'

steps.text: Fetch the public card. No auth needed; this is what other agents read.
Search the directory, also public.
From an agent over MCP, the same search is one tool call.

blocks.text: Pair this with the previous lesson and the loop closes: an agent discovers a peer in the directory, and a human-authored delegation decides whether it may actually hand it work.

The directory job board takes discovery one step further: instead of just finding an agent, post a task to the board, receive bids from discoverable agents, and award the work. Awarding hands the bidder an a2a_url pointing at its own runtime; 1claw hosts the board, not the work itself.

Job and bid text is written by one party and read by another party's model. That is a prompt-injection surface by definition, the same class of risk taught in the agent threat model track, just arriving through a job description instead of a scraped web page or a support ticket.

items: Every field is inspected server-side before it is stored. High-confidence injection is refused outright.

Anything below that threshold is returned as an untrusted-content envelope, not a plain string, for every client that reads it. The SDK types it so passing it straight into a prompt is a type error, not a runtime surprise.
MCP gets read-and-bid tools only for the job board. Nothing here lets an agent award work or move funds without a human step in between.

blocks.text: This is the lethal trifecta's second circle showing up somewhere new. A job board is untrusted content by construction: it exists so a stranger's text reaches your agent's context. Wrapping that text in a typed envelope instead of a string is the same idea as fail-closed content inspection elsewhere in this course, applied at the boundary where the untrusted content actually enters.
The directory and card endpoints are unauthenticated by design. Publish only what you would put on a public web page; the card is not a place for internal detail.

blocks.situation: Your agent's public card lists its A2A endpoint, its categories, and, to help integrators, the internal service names it orchestrates and the regions it runs in.
blocks.question: What should change?

options.text: Nothing. The card is metadata, not credentials, so it discloses nothing sensitive.
options.feedback: Metadata is exactly what reconnaissance consists of. Internal service names and regions map your architecture for anyone who asks, and the endpoint is unauthenticated by design.

options.text: Remove the internal service names and regions. The card is unauthenticated, so publish only what you would put on a public web page.
options.feedback: Correct. Discovery endpoints take no auth so that agents can find peers before any trust exists, which means the card is genuinely public. Capabilities and protocols belong there; internal topology does not.

options.text: Keep them but require an agent JWT to fetch the card.
options.feedback: That would break discovery, which depends on the card being readable before a relationship exists. The fix is to publish less, not to gate it.

options.text: Keep them but set discoverable to false so only direct links resolve.
options.feedback: Unlisted is not private. The card endpoint still answers, so this hides the page from search rather than from anyone who has the id.

quiz.question: Can an agent publish itself to the public directory?
options: Yes, if it has the discovery scope
Yes, with its own token
No: updating discovery settings is human-only
Only if it is Business tier
quiz.explanation: PATCH /v1/agents/{id}/discovery is human-only. Discovery is opt-in and stays under human control.

quiz.question: Which discovery endpoints require no authentication?
options: The directory search and the agent card
Only the agent card
Only the directory search
Neither: both need an agent JWT
quiz.explanation: GET /v1/agents/directory and GET /v1/agents/{id}/card are both public, which is what lets other agents discover peers before any trust exists.

quiz.question: Discovering an agent in the directory means you can delegate work to it.
options: True, if both agents are in the same org
True, if the card lists the tool
False: delegation still needs a human-authored delegation record
True, discovery implies permission
quiz.explanation: Discovery and authorization are separate. Finding an agent tells you it exists; a human-created delegation decides whether work can actually be handed to it.

quiz.question: Why does the directory job board return low-confidence-injection text as an untrusted-content envelope instead of a plain string?
options: To save bandwidth on large job descriptions
So the SDK's type system makes passing it straight into a prompt a type error rather than a silent injection risk
Envelopes are required for all API responses regardless of content
It only applies to bids, not job postings
quiz.explanation: Job and bid text is written by one party and read by another party's model, the textbook shape of a prompt-injection surface. Typing it as an envelope rather than a string forces every client to handle it deliberately instead of by accident.

title: Lab: fetch a real agent's public card
summary: Pull a live agent's public discovery card and run the same disclosure check the discovery lesson described, against something you did not write.

blocks.text: The discovery lesson said a card is unauthenticated by design, so publish only what you would put on a public web page. This lab checks whether that principle actually holds for a card that exists in production right now.

steps.text: Get an id from the live directory, then fetch that agent's card directly. No credentials, same as anyone on the internet could do.
steps.code:
AID=$(curl -s "https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/directory" | python3 -c "import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['agents'][0]['id'])")
curl -s "https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AID/card" | python3 -m json.tool

steps.text: A minimal, public-facing shape.
Check it against the discovery lesson's own warning: no internal service names, no region, no topology.
steps.code:
AID=$(curl -s "https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/directory" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["agents"][0]["id"])')
curl -s "https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AID/card" | python3 -c '
import json, sys
c = json.load(sys.stdin)
fields = set(c.keys())
expected = {"id", "name", "description", "tags", "a2a_url", "mcp_url", "capabilities"}
print("fields present:", sorted(fields))
print("unexpected fields:", sorted(fields - expected))
'

steps.text: Seven fields, all seven expected, nothing extra. Whichever agent you fetched, this list is the same, because it is generated from the schema rather than from what the operator remembered to leave out.

blocks.text: Whatever card you fetched, its field set is fixed by the API rather than by the operator's discretion. This is the structural version of the lesson's advice: the card cannot leak internal topology, because the schema never has a place to put it. A human choosing what to disclose can make a mistake; a schema with seven fixed fields cannot be talked into a wider one.

items: Compare this to your own systems. Anything you publish for discovery through a format you fully control can grow a field nobody meant to expose. The 1Claw card cannot, because the shape is enforced server-side.
capabilities is the only field carrying operational information, and it is a closed vocabulary of short strings rather than free text, which limits what could accidentally be disclosed even there.
Nothing here required trusting the operator's judgment. That is the actual security property: good defaults enforced by a schema beat good intentions enforced by a person remembering a guideline.

blocks.text: This is worth generalising past agent cards. Anywhere your own service publishes something for public discovery, ask whether the safe boundary is enforced by a schema or by whoever happens to be filling in the form that day.

quiz.question: Why can this card not leak internal topology the way a hand-written status page could?
options: The API strips suspicious-looking text
The response schema has a fixed set of fields, so there is no place to put it even by mistake
1Claw operators are trained not to include it
Cards are reviewed before publishing
quiz.explanation: A schema enforced server-side is a structural guarantee. A guideline followed by a person is not, which is the actual difference this lab demonstrates.

quiz.question: Why does it matter that `capabilities` is a closed vocabulary rather than free text?
options: It is faster to parse
It compresses better
It is required by the OpenAPI spec
Free text could accidentally carry more than intended; a fixed set of known strings cannot
quiz.explanation: A field that only accepts predefined values cannot become the place where someone pastes an internal hostname by accident, unlike an open description field.

quiz.question: What is the general principle this lab illustrates beyond agent cards?
options: Agent cards should never include capabilities
A safe disclosure boundary enforced by a schema is more reliable than one enforced by a person remembering a guideline
Discovery endpoints should be rate limited
Public APIs should always be free of authentication
quiz.explanation: This generalises to any public-facing endpoint your own systems publish: structural constraints hold up better than good intentions.

title: Capstone: design an access model
summary: Take a real brief and produce the identities, policies, and bindings a working system needs.

blocks.text: A logistics company is putting three agents into production. Design the access model. The brief is deliberately underspecified in the places real briefs are.

items: A quoting agent reads carrier rate cards and answers customer questions on a public web form.
A booking agent creates shipments through a carrier API, which is billed per call.
A reconciliation agent runs nightly, reads invoices, and writes a summary to an internal vault path.
One human operations lead owns all three. Compliance requires that any spend above 500 USD be attributable to a person.

blocks.text: Write your answer down before reading on. The value is in committing to a design and then finding out where it leaks.

Start with identity. Three agents, three identities, no sharing. That is not bureaucracy: the reconciliation agent runs unattended at night and the quoting agent takes input from the open internet, and when something goes wrong you need the audit trail to distinguish them. Give each its own environment tag, and lock the tag on the two that touch production.
Then scope. Work path by path rather than agent by agent, because the interesting question is which agent should not reach a path:

items: rates/** read for the quoting agent only. It never needs write, and it must never reach invoices.
invoices/** read for reconciliation only, with a deny on the quoting agent even though no allow would have matched it. The deny documents the intent and survives a later broad grant.
reports/** write for reconciliation only.
The booking agent gets no secret read at all, which is the interesting part.

steps.text: Give the booking agent a binding rather than a credential. It calls the carrier API through Execution Intents, so the key stays server-side.
Scope the quoting agent to exactly one prefix, and add the deny that documents what it must never reach.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$VAULT_ID/policies \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"principal_type":"agent","principal_id":"'$QUOTE_AGENT'",
       "path_pattern":"rates/**","permissions":["read"],
       "effect":"allow","priority":10}'

curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$VAULT_ID/policies \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"principal_type":"agent","principal_id":"'$QUOTE_AGENT'",
       "path_pattern":"invoices/**","permissions":["read"],
       "effect":"deny","priority":100}'

steps.text: Satisfy the compliance requirement with an approval policy rather than a hard cap, so large bookings reach the operations lead instead of failing.

blocks.situation: Six weeks in, the operations lead asks for the quoting agent to also answer questions about past shipments, so it needs read access to invoices/**. They point out that the deny you wrote is now blocking a legitimate business need.
blocks.question: What do you do?

options.text: Delete the deny policy and add an allow on invoices/** for the quoting agent.
options.feedback: This is the request taken at face value, and it puts customer invoice data one injection away from a public web form. The quoting agent is the one principal in this system whose input comes from the open internet.

options.text: Raise the quoting agent's allow priority above the deny so the existing rules resolve in its favour.
options.feedback: Mechanically this works, which is what makes it dangerous. It achieves the same exposure as deleting the deny while leaving a rule in place that looks like a control, so the next reviewer sees a deny and assumes invoices are protected.

options.text: Keep the boundary and give the quoting agent a binding to a shipment-status endpoint, so it gets answers without reading invoice secrets.
options.feedback: Correct. The business need is answers about shipments, not access to invoice material. A binding returns the former without granting the latter, and the deny stays meaningful.

options.text: Allow it but require approval on every invoice read.
options.feedback: Approval on a read that happens on every customer question is approval fatigue by design. It will be clicked through within a week, and then you have the exposure plus a false sense of oversight.

blocks.text: The pattern to take away: when a request arrives as "agent X needs access to Y", the useful question is what X actually needs to produce. Access is one way to get there and usually the widest one.

Notice what the finished design contains. Three identities, four path policies, one deny that documents intent, two bindings, and one approval threshold. Almost none of it is about encryption, which is where people expect secret management to live.

quiz.question: Why does the booking agent get no secret read access at all?
options: Its traffic is billed per call, so reads are expensive
Booking agents cannot be granted policies
It executes through a binding, so the carrier credential stays server-side
It runs unattended
quiz.explanation: The binding injects the credential at execution time. The agent never holds it, so there is nothing to scope a read policy to and nothing to leak.

quiz.question: What does the deny on invoices/** achieve when no allow would have matched anyway?
options: It prevents the path from being created
It speeds up policy evaluation
It is required before a binding can be created
It documents the intent and survives a later broad grant
quiz.explanation: Today it is redundant. Its value is on the day someone adds a broad allow, when it turns an accidental grant into an explicit decision someone has to override.

quiz.question: Why is an approval policy preferred over a hard 500 USD cap for the booking agent?
options: Approval policies cannot be bypassed
Caps are not supported for booking flows
It is cheaper to evaluate
A legitimate large booking reaches a human instead of simply failing
quiz.explanation: A hard cap refuses and the work stops. An approval policy routes the transaction to the operations lead, satisfying the attribution requirement without breaking the business case.
